result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.find_minimal_d_separator()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a minimal set of nodes that d-separates two others in a directed acyclic graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L45927-L46011){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.find_minimal_d_separator( x, y, included=None, restricted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Find minimal d-separator](/assets/graphs/find-minimal-d-separator.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A causal graph: age (teal) affects exercise, exercise affects weight, and both exercise and weight affect heart health (violet). Every path from age to heart starts with the edge into exercise, so conditioning on exercise alone, in the accent color, blocks them all. The card returns the minimal separator [exercise]." width="100%"} Returns a minimal d-separator of `x` and `y` (see `is_d_separator()` and `is_minimal_d_separator()`): a set of nodes that, once conditioned on, blocks every path between them, and from which no node can be dropped. In causal inference this is a lean set of variables to measure or adjust for. Constraints mirror real studies: `included=` forces variables into the set (for example, ones that are always recorded) and `restricted=` limits the set to observable variables. When `x` and `y` are adjacent, or every separator would need a forbidden node, no separator exists and `None` is returned. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [x]{.doc-parameter-name} : Nodes, or lists of nodes, as IDs or labels. [y]{.doc-parameter-name} : Nodes, or lists of nodes, as IDs or labels. [included]{.doc-parameter-name}[=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op}[None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional nodes that must be in the separator. [restricted]{.doc-parameter-name}[=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op}[None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional nodes that the separator may use (default: all nodes). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int] or None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node IDs of a minimal separator, sorted, or `None` if none exists. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is not a directed acyclic graph, a node does not exist, `x`, `y` and `included` overlap, or `included` is not part of `restricted`. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The linear-time algorithm of van der Zander, Liśkiewicz and Textor (2019), as in NetworkX: start from all allowed ancestors of `x`, `y` and `included`, keep those reachable from `x` by open paths, then those also reachable from `y`. Each step is a graph search, so the whole computation runs in $O(V + E)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Age influences heart health only through exercise (directly, and via weight), so conditioning on exercise alone separates them: ::: {#2f28e094 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["age", "exercise", "weight", "heart"]) g.add_edges([("age", "exercise"), ("exercise", "weight"), ("weight", "heart"), ("exercise", "heart")]) [g.get_label_from_id(n) for n in g.find_minimal_d_separator("age", "heart")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['exercise'] ``` ::: ::: With a direct edge from age to heart health, nothing can separate them: ::: {#72c1d7d7 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.add_edge("age", "heart") g.find_minimal_d_separator("age", "heart") is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` True ``` ::: :::
